questions.q: A package fails immediately with a 'Login timeout expired' error naming a connection manager. Which failure category is this?
options: Connection failure
Data type mismatch
Permission issue
Downstream/dependency failure
questions.explain: Errors that name the connection manager itself and occur right at the start of a task, before any real row processing, are classic connection failures.

questions.q: Which Chapter 6 tool is the most direct fix for a data type mismatch on a specific column mid-data-flow?
options: Error outputs — redirect the bad rows instead of failing the whole load
Checkpoints — restart the package from the point of failure
Event handlers — send an e-mail when the error occurs
Logging providers — write the event to a text file
questions.explain: Error outputs (Lesson 32) exist specifically to redirect rows that fail conversion or truncation instead of letting one bad value fail the entire Data Flow task.

questions.q: A package works fine when run manually from SSDT, but fails once deployed and run by the SQL Server Agent service account. What category of failure is this most likely?
options: Permission issue — the account actually executing the package lacks rights the developer's account had
Data type mismatch
Connection failure
It cannot be a real failure since the package logic never changed
questions.explain: This is the signature of a permission issue: the package's logic is fine, but the account running it in production has different access than the account used during development.

questions.q: Which logging categories are most useful for diagnosing a permission-related failure?
options: Operator and SourceName — to see which account and which step actually failed
DataBytes — reserved for future use and rarely populated
ExecutionID only, since it uniquely identifies a single run
Logging provides no information relevant to permission issues
questions.explain: Operator identifies which account ran the package, and SourceName identifies which task or container failed — exactly the information needed to diagnose a permission mismatch.

questions.q: Why is 'just rerun the package' usually not a real fix for connection, data type, permission, or dependency failures?
options: Rerunning without changing anything reproduces the same underlying problem, unless the failure was genuinely transient
SSIS packages can only be executed successfully once per day
Rerunning a package always deletes the checkpoint file automatically
Rerunning without a checkpoint is technically impossible in SSIS
questions.explain: None of the four categories are caused by randomness — rerunning without addressing the connection, mismatch, permission, or dependency issue just reproduces the same failure, except for genuinely transient problems.
